title: The Three Corollaries: Constant, Difference Constant, Monotone
quickIdea: f' = 0 everywhere makes f constant, f' = g' makes f - g constant, and the sign of f' decides whether f rises or falls. All three are the mean value theorem applied between two arbitrary points.
remember: If f'(x) = 0 for every x in (a, b) then f is constant on [a, b]: apply the theorem between any two points and the difference is f'(c)(x2 - x1) = 0.
If f'(x) = g'(x) on an interval then f - g is constant there, so two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant.
If f' > 0 on (a, b) then f is strictly increasing; f' < 0 strictly decreasing; f' >= 0 non-decreasing.
The converses fail: x^3 is strictly increasing on the whole line and f'(0) = 0.
These corollaries are what make the first-derivative test and the constant-of-integration rule valid rather than merely plausible.

example.prompt: Show that f(x) = x^3 + 2x + 5 is strictly increasing on the whole real line.
example.work: f'(x) = 3x^2 + 2, and 3x^2 >= 0, so f'(x) >= 2 > 0 everywhere. Take any x1 < x2; the mean value theorem on [x1, x2] gives f(x2) - f(x1) = f'(c)(x2 - x1) with f'(c) > 0 and x2 - x1 > 0.
example.answer: f(x2) > f(x1) for every x1 < x2, so f is strictly increasing.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2020 Q.1 asks which of e^(-x), x^2 - sin x and sqrt(x^3 + 1) is increasing on [0, 1]. The route is this corollary: differentiate and read the sign, and note that x^2 - sin x has derivative 2x - cos x, which is -1 at 0, so it falls first and then rises.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2020 Q.1: which of I. e^(-x), II. x^2 - sin x, III. sqrt(x^3 + 1) is increasing everywhere in [0, 1]?
variations.why: The derivative of I is -e^(-x) < 0, so it decreases. The derivative of II is 2x - cos x, which is -1 at x = 0 and about 1.46 at x = 1, so II decreases first. The derivative of III is 3x^2/(2 sqrt(x^3 + 1)), positive for x > 0, so III increases.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: If f'(x) = g'(x) for every x, f(0) = 4 and g(0) = 1, what is f(1) - g(1)?
variations.why: f - g has zero derivative everywhere, so it is constant; its value at 0 is 3 and therefore its value at 1 is 3. The variation is the constant-of-integration corollary in disguise.

trap.what: Concluding 'strictly increasing' from f' >= 0, or 'increasing' from f'(p) > 0 at one point p.
trap.why: f' >= 0 gives only non-decreasing - a constant function satisfies it. And a positive derivative at a single point says nothing about a neighbourhood unless f' stays positive near p.
trap.counterexample: f(x) = 5 has f' = 0 >= 0 everywhere and is not strictly increasing. For the pointwise version, f(x) = x^3 - 3x has f'(-2) = 9 > 0 but f decreases on (-1, 1).

check.question: Is f(x) = x + sin x increasing on the whole real line?
check.explanation: f'(x) = 1 + cos x >= 0, and it is zero only at odd multiples of pi, isolated points. On any interval between two such points f' > 0, so f is strictly increasing on each and therefore on the whole line.
